source: Russell (1997) Metareasoning (MIT Encyclopedia of Cognitive Sciences entry; summarises Russell and Wefald 1989/1991)
finding: Rational metareasoning treats a computation as an action. Its benefit is a possibly better external decision. Its cost is delay. The metalevel picks computations by expected value and decides when computation should give way to action. Roots are I. J. Good's Type II rationality and Howard's information value theory.
numbers: Worked example: action A looks worth 10 (sd 1), B worth 8 (sd 4). Expected value of computation is 0.3 for lookahead from A and 0.82 from B.
quote: a computation can be viewed as an action whose benefit is that it may result in better external decisions
limits: Tutorial-level text; the full derivation is in the 1991 book, which was not opened.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact stop rule we can code: stop when no available step has positive value minus cost.

source: Russell (1997) Metareasoning (MIT Encyclopedia of Cognitive Sciences entry; summarises Russell and Wefald 1989/1991)
finding: Value of computation depends on whether a clear choice has already emerged. It falls when one option leads clearly, and is near zero when the options are close and it does not matter which is picked.
numbers: A=12 instead of 10: VOC drops from 0.3 and 0.82 to 0.002 and 0.06. Both options 10 with sd 0.1: VOC 0.03.
limits: Toy numbers from a two-action lookahead, not an empirical test.
agent_relevance: Supports a program-side stop rule: stop when the leader margin is large (VOC small) or when options are tied and the choice does not matter. Spend on close races with a big utility gap.

source: Russell (1997) Metareasoning (MIT Encyclopedia of Cognitive Sciences entry; summarises Russell and Wefald 1989/1991)
finding: Anytime algorithms have a performance profile (quality vs time). With a known profile, the metalevel choice of which algorithm to run and when to stop is fairly trivial. Finer control scores single steps. Soar compiles the result of subgoaling into a rule to avoid re-deliberating (chunking).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Profile must be known or estimated; for LLM reasoning the profile is per problem and unknown in advance.
agent_relevance: A per-problem-class accuracy-vs-samples profile (from our own logs) is the cheapest usable VOC model for the S0 gate. Chunking link: see the Soar chunking subfield.

source: Hay, Russell, Tolpin, Shimony (2012) Selecting Computations: Theory and Applications
finding: Formal metalevel decision problem (Bayesian selection). The myopic policy (Russell and Wefald's one-step meta-greedy) stops too early, but if myopic does a computation the optimal policy also does one (Theorem 7). Optimal policy's expected number of computations is bounded by value of perfect information times 1/c (Theorem 5). A simple counterexample shows an optimal policy need not reach a decision in all cases.
numbers: One-armed Bernoulli problem with constant arm: at most (1-lambda)/c - 3 <= 1/(4c) - 3 computations (Theorem 10). Blinkered policy is computed in time linear in number of arms (Theorem 16); Q_myopic <= Q_blinkered <= Q_optimal.
quote: The myopic policy is an extreme approximation, often stopping far too early.
limits: Theory for independent actions and flat selection; Go and Bernoulli experiments only; applicability to free-text reasoning is by analogy.
agent_relevance: Gives a proven bound: sample budget scales as 1/cost. Also says a one-step stop rule ('would one more sample change the vote?') is safe for continuing but unsafe for stopping. Use a deeper lookahead (blinkered per candidate answer).

source: Hay et al. (2012) Selecting Computations
finding: Blinkered policy was compared with bandit-style (UCB1) and value-of-information heuristics on Bernoulli sampling with k=25 arms over a wide range of step costs c. Metalevel VOI methods beat bandit heuristics in one-shot decisions and in Go.
numbers: Bernoulli sampling, k=25 arms; regret axis about 0.002 to 0.05 (figure labels). Exact win rates not extracted.
limits: Only figure labels and text read; exact table values were not recovered.
agent_relevance: Supports VOI-style stopping rather than UCB-style sampling when the goal is one decision, not total reward.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Strategy selection as rational metareasoning, Psychological Review 124, 762-794
finding: People pick the strategy with the best predicted speed-accuracy trade-off: VOC(s, problem) = expected utility of the action the strategy picks minus cost, with cost = time cost x execution time. Strategies are chosen from learned predictions that use problem features, with Thompson-sampling exploration. Lesion tests: features and VOC selection were essential; exploration and separate time/reward models were needed in later experiments.
numbers: Model: argmax over mappings from features to strategies of expected VOC. Compared against SSL, RELACS and SCADS, 14 alternative models in Exps 2 and 3.
limits: Tasks are sorting and gambles with MTurk adults; strategies are explicit, not free thinking. Model predicted effects were slightly larger than observed.
agent_relevance: Our agent should select a reasoning strategy per problem from observable problem features (not a single average best), and learn the cost and success of each strategy separately. This is the theory behind G12.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Exp. 1, sorting
finding: Participants chose between cocktail sort and merge sort for lists that differed in length and presortedness. Context-free learners (SSL, RELACS) predicted wrong because cocktail sort was faster on most training lists but much slower on long, nearly inverted test lists. People chose adaptively on feature-dependent lists.
numbers: 100 MTurk participants, 18 test lists. People chose adaptively on 83.0% of trials; rational metareasoning predicted 70.5% (+/-3.2), t(298)=2.34, p<0.01; SSL, RELACS and SCADS lower (p<0.001).
limits: Qualitatively adaptive but people beat the model; merge sort chosen for long inverted lists, not for short or presorted lists.
agent_relevance: Average-case rules (always sample N) fail when problem classes differ; use problem features to set effort.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Exp. 2
finding: When deliberation costs more than it earns, people learn to think less: they inspect fewer payoffs, skip hopeless problems and choose at random when all outcomes are good, while reward per decision stays about the same.
numbers: N=100 MTurk. Reward rate up t(99)=9.98, d=1.00; information acquisitions down t(99)=4.80, d=0.48; engagement down t(98)=7.89, d=0.79; engaged trials fell from 37% to 19%; reward per decision unchanged t(98)=0.69, p=0.49.
limits: Short laboratory task, small-stakes gambles.
agent_relevance: Evidence that cutting effort when it does not pay is learnable and costs little accuracy, in line with the LLM stopping results.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Exp. 3
finding: When the environment changed so low-stakes problems became the only way to earn, people learned to deliberate more, engaging more often and gathering more information. Observed effects were slightly smaller than predicted.
numbers: 200 model simulations per alternative; the model engaged in 20 to 30% more problems and acquired about 0.5 to 3 more pieces of information than people. Only the full model captured Exps 2 and 3 together.
limits: Learning in people is slower than the ideal learner.
agent_relevance: Effort policy must update both ways: lower when wasted, higher when the problem class is now worth it. A stop rule that only cuts is incomplete.

source: Lieder and Griffiths (2017) Exp. 4, adaptive flexibility
finding: In a 50/50 mix of problems where take-the-best and weighted-additive strategies give opposite answers, context-free learners fall to chance and feature-based learners stay above 60%. People matched the strategy to the problem on most trials.
numbers: N=100, 100 binary choices each; people agreed with the appropriate strategy on 76.2% of trials; simulated feature-based model above 60%, SSL and RELACS at chance.
limits: Strategies and features were given in the interface.
agent_relevance: Per-problem strategy switching beats one best average strategy, as long as a cue for which strategy applies is available.

source: Callaway, Gul, Krueger, Griffiths, Lieder (2018) Learning to select computations (BMPS)
finding: Bayesian metalevel policy search approximates optimal computation selection by mixing myopic value of information and value of perfect information. Tested on stopping, allocation across options and planning, near optimal in all three.
numbers: Only the abstract page was read: near-optimal on three metareasoning problems.
limits: Full paper not read.
agent_relevance: Practical recipe for a learned stop rule with few parameters instead of full dynamic programming.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: Transfers VOC to LLM training. Reward of a chain of thought z is R = U(z|x,y) - C(z), with utility = log pi(y|z,x) - log pi(y|x) (gain in answer likelihood) and cost = lambda x chain length. Expert Iteration keeps chains with positive advantage. No outside reward model.
numbers: Four train sets x 1024 samples = 4096 items; eval on ARC, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, ProofWriter; Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B and instruct variants.
limits: Requires fine-tuning and a known target answer; our scaffold does not train. Few-shot baselines used long prompts.
agent_relevance: VOC as a reward needs only answer likelihood and length. In a no-training scaffold it can be a per-chain score used for selection or for deciding to stop sampling.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2025) RaM results, Table 1
finding: RaM cut output tokens vs STaR while holding or raising accuracy.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B: RaM 50.1% / 170.8 output tokens vs STaR 47.4% / 222.7 vs few-shot CoT 34.8% / 261.9 (as printed in the first model block). Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: RaM 63.5% / 146.2 vs STaR 61.9% / 215.1. Overall 23 to 32% fewer tokens than STaR and 35 to 42% fewer than few-shot CoT.
limits: Table layout in the PDF is garbled; the model-to-row mapping is from reading order. Rescaled accuracy averaged over four datasets. Gains largest on tasks where chains add little.
agent_relevance: A learned effort policy can cut tokens a lot without losing accuracy on easy tasks.

source: De Sabbata et al. (2025) RaM adaptivity, Table 2 and out-of-distribution
finding: Hard/easy split = whether direct answering was right. RaM widened the length gap between hard and easy items; the instruct model with plain CoT did not adapt at all. Out of distribution on MMLU-CF RaM kept accuracy with 28 to 36% fewer tokens than STaR; physics and engineering saved less.
numbers: Length reduction easy vs hard: RaM 50.3% and 36.0%, STaR 34.4% and 35.9%, instruct CoT 0.5% and 0.9%. Hard 145 vs easy 72 tokens for RaM in the first block.
limits: Easy/hard is defined by direct-answer success, a proxy. Cites Sprague et al. 2024: CoT mainly helps maths and logic.
agent_relevance: Plain instruction-tuned models do not scale their thinking to difficulty; the scaffold must supply that signal (G11, G12).

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Sampling many chains and majority voting beats greedy chain of thought. Gains saturate fast, and vote share tracks accuracy, which is the seed of every confidence-based stop rule.
numbers: PaLM-540B with 40 paths: GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4, SVAMP 79.0 to 86.6, AQuA 35.8 to 48.3, StrategyQA 75.3 to 81.6, ARC-c 85.2 to 88.7. 5 to 10 paths capture much of the gain.
limits: Read via a fetched HTML summary. Fixed budget per question; agreement is not independent evidence (our G4).
agent_relevance: Baseline we compare stopping rules against; vote share as a stop signal is a hint only.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency (EMNLP)
finding: Sample one answer at a time. After each, compute the probability that the current leader stays the majority; stop when it passes a threshold. The Dirichlet form is costly, so the main method uses a Beta approximation comparing the top two answers with a non-informative Beta(1,1) prior and threshold 0.95.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs (Vicuna-13B, code-davinci-002, GPT-3.5-Turbo), max 40 samples. Maths: 3.3x fewer samples, -0.1 acc. Commonsense 2.9x, -0.2. Symbolic 3.8x, 0.0. Code 2.4x, +0.4. Per model: GPT-3.5 4.4x, Vicuna 1.9x, code-davinci 3.4x. Up to 7.9x on Boolean expressions with no loss; SVAMP under 5 samples on average.
limits: Weaker model (Vicuna) saves least, 21.7 of 40 samples. Authors note the rule can fire when the majority is unstable; assumes independent samples.
agent_relevance: Directly usable stop rule at S3/S7; run it on counted answer equality, which fits G5.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency analysis
finding: At matched average cost, adaptive sampling beats fixed self-consistency because it spends more where agreement is hard to reach. Stopping rules compared: random, majority-at-threshold, entropy, Beta, Dirichlet, Chinese restaurant process. Beta, Dirichlet and CRP are similar in accuracy; Beta runs about four orders of magnitude faster than Dirichlet and CRP.
numbers: At average cost 10 samples, about 3% higher accuracy on GSM8K; up to 5 points absolute across datasets. Paired tests: accuracy p average 0.50 (no difference), generations p average 1.5e-3.
limits: Cost counted in samples, not tokens; answers with different rationale lengths cost differently.
agent_relevance: Allocate by agreement, not uniformly: this is G12 in practice. Stop rules cost almost nothing next to a model call.

source: Li, Yuan, Feng, Pan, Wang, Sun, Wang, Li (2024) Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), ICLR
finding: Split the sample budget L into windows of size w. Stop as soon as all w answers in one window agree (zero entropy). A theory section shows the stopped answer matches the full-vote answer with high probability; a control scheme predicts cost and accuracy change from the first window.
numbers: Sampling reductions: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%. GPT-4 on MATH: SC 60.32 vs ESC 59.98 at about 42.4 of 64 samples; w=8 for MATH, 5 elsewhere; L=64 or 40. Voting results of ESC and SC agree 99.1 to 99.96% (GSM8K, SQA, Letter).
limits: Weak models save almost nothing: Llama-2-7B on MATH used 62.48 of 64 samples (accuracy 7.7). Savings correlate with accuracy. Control scheme predictions had Pearson r above 0.8.
agent_relevance: Cheapest rule to implement (one window of identical answers). Expect little saving exactly where the model is weak, which is where search is needed (G12 foothold).

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC robustness and cost
finding: ESC works across window sizes, max sample sizes, temperatures, zero-shot prompts and a code task (MBPP). The window can share one prompt so input tokens are paid once per window.
numbers: GPT-4 MATH, w=8: L=16 uses 13.56 samples, L=40 uses 28.49, L=64 uses 42.41, same accuracy to 0.01; GPT-3.5-Turbo L=64 uses 52.37 samples.
limits: Conservative rule (all in window equal) means savings shrink as L grows on hard items; averaged over 10 runs, variance not reported.
agent_relevance: Choose window w by model strength; w=5 to 8.

source: Taubenfeld, Sheffer, Ofek, Feder, Goldstein, Gekhman, Yona (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency (CISC)
finding: Weight each sampled path by model-given confidence. This reaches the same accuracy with fewer paths. The best confidence signal was P(True) with normalisation, and a new metric, within-question discrimination, shows confidence separates right from wrong paths for the same question.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets. Cost reduction at budget 10: P(True) 46%, response probability 31%, verbal 1-100 30%, verbal binary 10%. Average over 40%, some above 67%. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 73% cost reduction.
limits: Needs an extra confidence call or logprobs; within-question discrimination is modest (about 62% for P(True)); it is weighting, not early stopping.
agent_relevance: Confidence weighting is a second lever beside stopping, but G5 says a model must not judge its own answer; only use logprobs computed by code.

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys
finding: Coverage (fraction of problems with at least one correct sample) grows roughly log-linearly with number of samples over orders of magnitude. With a verifier, coverage converts into accuracy. Without one, voting plateaus far below coverage.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% at 1 sample, 56% at 250 samples (single-sample SOTA 43%). MATH with Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples, 98.44% at 10,000; majority voting or reward models only 40.50% to 41.41%. Gemma-2B CodeContests: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000.
limits: Needs an automatic verifier for gains; the voting plateau is the limit for consensus stopping.
agent_relevance: Consensus stop rules cap at the voting plateau. When we have a code-checkable test (G3), keep sampling by pass/fail, not by agreement.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Bin questions into five difficulty levels by the base model's pass rate; the best test-time strategy differs by bin. Easy questions: sequential revisions only. Hard: a mix of sequential and parallel. PRM beam search wins at low budget, best-of-N on easy items at high budget. On the hardest bin nothing helps.
numbers: MATH 500 questions, PaLM 2-S*, difficulty from 2048 samples per question. Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute (revisions 64 vs 256 samples; search 16 vs 64). Test-time compute beat a roughly 14x larger model on easy and medium questions at low inference load (R=0.16); pretraining won on bins 4-5 and at high inference load (R=22).
limits: Read through a fetched HTML summary, not the full PDF. One model, one dataset. Predicted difficulty (verifier score) costs 2048 samples not counted in results. Beam search got worse with budget on levels 1-2 (PRM over-optimisation).
agent_relevance: Supports G12 and G11. The difficulty estimate must be cheap; a first-pass agreement score is a candidate.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Budget forcing ends thinking by force when over budget or lengthens it by appending 'Wait' when the model tries to stop. Compared with token-, step- and class-conditional length prompts and rejection sampling on AIME24, only budget forcing had perfect control and a positive slope. Prompted length limits were not obeyed.
numbers: s1-32B (Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, SFT on 1,000 samples, 26 min on 16 H100): AIME24 50% to 57% with forced Wait (2x, 4x, 6x). Table 3 AIME24: budget forcing control 100%, scaling slope 15, performance 56.7; token-conditional control 40%; class-conditional 50%; rejection sampling 100% control but negative slope (-35). Token prompting alone met its limit 2 of 5 times.
limits: Table 3 text layout is garbled; the BF row is clear, others partly inferred. Flattens at high budgets and is bounded by context window. 30 AIME problems only.
agent_relevance: A hard cap on thinking is a code-enforced budget, in line with G11; forced 'Wait' is a doubt trigger on a schedule and so conflicts with G1 unless a check fails.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1, limits of sequential scaling
finding: Budget forcing flattens out and is limited by context. Parallel scaling with tree search (REBASE with a process reward model) scaled better than majority voting and than sequential scaling at the highest budgets.
numbers: Budget forcing ablation on AIME24: no extrapolation 50.0; 2x without string 50.0; 2x 'Alternatively' 50.0 (MATH 92.2, GPQA 59.6). REBASE or majority over 16 parallel trajectories; sequential up to 512 steps.
limits: REBASE needs a reward-model pass not counted in thinking tokens.
agent_relevance: Prefer several short independent attempts to one long one (G11), and stop a chain by a hard cap.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models burn tokens on trivial questions and keep re-checking after a correct first answer. The first solution is correct in over 92% of cases. Self-training with shorter-sample preferences (SimPO + first-correct-solution + reflection) removes much of it.
numbers: '2+3': QwQ-32B-Preview produced 13 solutions in 901 tokens, first correct at 39 tokens; 1,953% more tokens than a conventional model. QwQ MATH500 2407.9 tokens, 3.2 solutions, outcome efficiency 52.3%. SimPO+FCS+Reflection: ASDIV 96.9 to 96.8 acc, 741.8 to 381.6 tokens (-48.6%); GSM8K 94.8 to 96.0, -46.1%; MATH500 93.0 to 92.8, -44.7%; GPQA 59.6 to 59.1, -35.4%; AIME24 46.7 to 43.3, -45.6%.
limits: Read via a fetched HTML summary. Reductions computed from table values. The intro says -48.6% on MATH500 but that number matches ASDIV; the first-correct-only variant lost 2 points on MATH500 (93.0 to 91.0 at -57.8%).
agent_relevance: Measures the price of no stopping rule. A cheap rule: stop after the first answer that passes a check, rather than re-solving.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses local token-level confidence (lowest sliding-window group confidence over 2,048-token windows) to cut low-quality traces during generation. Online: 16 warmup traces set a percentile threshold; sampling stops once vote consensus reaches 0.95 or the budget (512 traces) ends.
numbers: AIME 2025, GPT-OSS-120B no tools: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs majority 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%; DeepConf-low reached 97.9% with up to 84.7% fewer generated tokens. Token savings 43 to 79% (low) and 18 to 59% (high).
limits: Read via a fetched HTML summary (final 7% not read). Fails on confidently wrong traces: top-10% filtering helped in 12 of 20 settings and lost up to 4.69 points in eight; DeepConf-low lost about 4.4 points for Qwen3-8B on AIME25. Needs logprobs.
agent_relevance: Confidence is a hint, never proof (G4). It reduces cost but can lock in a shared wrong answer.

source: Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (RASC), arXiv 2408.17017
finding: Scores each sample (answer features plus reasoning features such as step count) with a logistic regression; stops when 5 samples score at least 0.5; final vote is score-weighted. Uses fewer samples than Adaptive-Consistency and ESC at similar accuracy.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo maths: RASC 6.62 samples vs ESC 14.94 vs AC 12.49; accuracy 69.4 vs 69.3 vs 67.6. Cuts vs SC (40) about 83 to 90% for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, 73 to 80% for Vicuna and Llama2; accuracy within about 0.5 points, but Vicuna-13B -0.9 (commonsense) and -2.0 (symbolic).
limits: Read via a fetched HTML summary. Abstract says about 70% and body says 60 to 80%; main table larger. Needs training data for the scorer. Author list not verified.
agent_relevance: A learned scorer beats pure agreement counts, but uses the model's reasoning text as a feature, which G10 warns about.

source: Liu, Qu, Schneider, Singh, Kumar (2025) CaRT: Teaching LLM agents to know when they know enough
finding: Models both overshoot and undershoot in information gathering. CaRT trains with counterfactual pairs: a trajectory where stopping is right and a minimal edit where it is not, plus verbal reasons for each. Ablations: counterfactual data gave the biggest gain, reasoning traces added a consistent further gain.
numbers: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, medical diagnosis dialogue and math. Termination labelled when answer success rate rises by at least 50% (positive) and counterfactual drops below 30%. Final dataset 80% continue and 20% terminate. Base and SFT models did worse than a fixed-questions rule out of distribution (dermatology); CaRT beat it. RL post-training lengthened conversations.
limits: Only text and ablation description read; exact success-rate numbers were not extracted. Small model; success labels come from an outside model over 50 generations.
agent_relevance: Stopping can be trained from counterfactual pairs; in a no-training agent the same idea is a test: would one more step change the checked answer?

source: Russell and Wefald (1991) Do the Right Thing: Studies in Limited Rationality, MIT Press (known here only via Russell 1997 and Hay et al. 2012)
finding: Original source of the value-of-computation and meta-greedy single-step approximation, applied to game-tree search. Not opened; described through two secondary documents that were read.
numbers: None extracted from the book.
limits: Book not opened; claims here are only as reported by Russell (1997) and Hay et al. (2012).
agent_relevance: Cite it as the origin but rely on the two read documents for any detail.
